newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lacroix's chaos perks up fashion week.
newsitem.headline: Lacroix's chaos perks up fashion week.

text.p: Christian Lacroix snapped the fashion crowd out of its torpor at the weekend with an outrageous riot of colour and a chaotic patchwork of genres that defied all the preset rules of establishment fashion.

From a quilted harlequin coat matched with a fuschia and chartreuse dress of patchwork crochet to a lame jacket with foamy Mongolian lamb collar, blue lace mini and lime stockings, the outfits on Lacroix's Autumn Winter catwalk on Saturday seemed thrown together haphazardly from a thousand different inspirations.

He paired the blue suede trousers of a flower child with the damask jacket of a 18th century duchess or put the whalebone stays of a hoop skirt in the leg o'mutton sleeves of a black satin tunic, worn on a skirt encrusted with lace and pearls.
But his wacky collage of colours, fabrics and styles was as deliberately constructed as the orchid embroidered on a salmon taffeta evening dress or the lace-trimmed cuffs of a blue tweed jacket.

"It was very spirited," said Joan Kaner of Neiman Marcus department stores. "It was Lacroix at his zaniest and wittiest. The pieces were beautiful and he put them together in an amusing way. But we'll put them together differently for our customers."

Jean-Paul Gaultier brought streetwear to the catwalk late on Friday, showing high-topped sneakers left untied, hooded jersey sweaters and baggy, over-sized trousers in shimmering fabrics, pinstripes or mohair tartan for evening.
For rappers with well-stocked wallets there was a gold lame evening tunic over jogging pants and tennis shoes or a velvet gown slit open over knee socks and thick-soled combat boots.
Funky and fresh for evening were the "shroud of Turin" print coats or the electric yellow plaids on fringed velvet dresses.

At Vivienne Westwood, Jerry Hall emerged in a sequined stripper's bra and garters while supermodels pranced along the stage of a kitsch Paris nightclub with frizzed Mary Stuart hairdoes, garters and heaving breasts bulging from bustiers.

But what was left for the British designer's showroom once you took away the chastity belt underwear, a camel-hair suit with its skirt sliced well above the privates or an S&M series of draped latex cocktail dresses with heavy chain collars and leather paraphernalia with zippers in strategic places?
Perhaps the tailored tartan suits worn with pom-pom argyle socks, which were accompanied on the catwalk by a half-naked bagpipe player, or Victorian-style grey flannel suits with padded derrieres.
Ten years after Claude Montana put power-dressing on fashion's cutting edge, it's back in style.

His beautifully-executed and restrained collection was about perfection: from the razor-edged pleats of gabardine trousers to the kimono sleeves of his tailored jackets, not a thread was out of place.
While his power-shoulders popped on other catwalks, Montana softened his angular cut and ice maidens of the 1980s.

Sweeping coats dominated the runaway in cashmere, alpaca and wool-silk mixes. In mauve, ice blue, dove grey or chestnut, there were military duffles or sumptuous and dramatic versions with gently sloping hems.

Long wool Amazon skirts and smart jackets were reminiscent of 19th century rifing costumes, while evening wear had a special brand of romance in irridescent ruby taffeta and transparent veining on black velvet bodices.
"Beautiful," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue. "It's his time again."
